data.text:
Joseph Verbis Lafleur, born on January 24, 1912, in Ville Platte, Louisiana, was a Roman Catholic priest, U.S. Army chaplain, and World War II hero whose life exemplified unwavering faith, courage, and selflessness. The fourth of seven children, Lafleur grew up in a poor Cajun family, facing hardship after his father abandoned them. Despite these challenges, his mother, Agatha, nurtured his early calling to the priesthood, which he expressed as a young boy serving as an altar boy at age seven. This commitment led him to St. Joseph’s Minor Seminary and later Notre Dame Major Seminary in New Orleans, where he was ordained in 1938.

After serving as an assistant pastor at St. Mary Magdalen Church in Abbeville, Louisiana, Lafleur joined the U.S. Army Air Corps as a chaplain in 1941, driven by a desire to minister to soldiers during World War II. Stationed at Clark Field in the Philippines, he faced the Japanese attack on December 8, 1941, where his heroic actions—comforting the wounded, administering last rites, and leading prayers amid chaos—earned him the Distinguished Service Cross and Purple Heart. Captured after the fall of Corregidor in May 1942, Lafleur spent over two years as a Japanese prisoner of war, enduring harsh conditions in multiple camps.

As a POW, Lafleur’s ministry never faltered. He built a chapel called St. Peter in Chains, celebrated Mass, and provided spiritual and physical aid, often sacrificing his own food and medicine for others. His compassion inspired nearly 200 conversions to Catholicism among prisoners. In September 1944, aboard the SS Shinyo Maru, a Japanese “hell ship,” Lafleur died heroically, helping 83 fellow POWs escape after the ship was unknowingly torpedoed by a U.S. submarine. He refused to save himself, pushing others to safety under enemy fire, earning posthumous awards, including a second Distinguished Service Cross and Purple Heart in 2017.

On September 5, 2020, the Diocese of Lafayette opened Lafleur’s cause for canonization, granting him the title “Servant of God.” In 2021, U.S. bishops overwhelmingly supported advancing his path to sainthood, recognizing his heroic virtue. Today, Lafleur’s legacy endures through memorials, scholarships, and an annual Mass on September 7, his death anniversary, inspiring countless faithful with his model of sacrifice and devotion.

Lafleur’s life challenges the narrative of self-preservation, showing that true heroism lies in selfless love and faith, even in the face of unimaginable trials. His story, rooted in Cajun heritage and Catholic devotion, continues to resonate as a testament to the power of living for others.

[2:44PM] #Okota #Isolo #TrafficUpdate 

Traffic movement across the Okota and Isolo axis is generally smooth this evening. Cele inward towards Ago Roundabout is free-flowing, with the return journey equally good. The Cele Link Bridge inward to Ijesha, providing access to Ijesha Market, is clear in both directions. Similarly, the inner part of Nwachukwu Drive connecting to Cele is also good to go, inward and outward.

Along Ago Palace Way, movement towards  Apple Junction remains encouraging at this time. The Ibeh, Apata, and Transformer Junction corridors inward to Ilasa Service Lane are clear, with no obstruction in the return flow. The inner part of Ire Akari linking Osolo Road is also free in both directions.

Chemist inward towards Pako is moving smoothly, as is the return route. The Oke Afa stretch towards Lasutech Roundabout is also clear in both directions. Daleko Bridge inward towards Palm Avenue records no delay, with return movement equally free. Furthermore, traffic around Five Star and Iyana Isolo inward towards Ijesha Express—both on the main carriageway and service lane—is currently good to go, with no reported impediments for now.
Our men are present at important locations ensuring ease of traffic movement.
